26.0.0.en: 1 But Job answered and said, 2 "How hast thou helped him that is without power? how savest thou the arm that hath no strength? 3 How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom? and how hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is? 4 To whom hast thou uttered words? and whose spirit came from thee?"

26.1.0.en: How hast thou helped him that is without power? how savest thou the arm that hath no strength? [2]

26.1.1.en: Job addresses Bildad in an eloquent and splendid style, with humility and contrition. Job counts himself as one with "no power," and his arm as one with "no strength," and in mockery he says to Bildad: What a helper you are of him who has no power, and a strengthener of the arms that have no strength! While confessing his own extreme weakness, he rebukes Bildad, who thinks himself wise, a guide and a helper, yet is in fact crushing the spirit of him who has no power and of him whose arm has no strength.

26.1.2.en: Here Job exposes Bildad, showing that, like his two companions, he has spoken eloquent words and sincere truths of faith, but what he has offered is talk without love and dialogue without action. What he has offered does not help him who has no power, nor does it support an arm that has no strength.

26.1.3.en: * (Job says) But I do not blame you for defending the role of God, for this is needed. In any case, you ought not to condemn me, although, in truth, it should have been possible to defend the grace of God without subjecting Job to so many accusations.

26.1.4.en: St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that it was fitting for Bildad (and his two companions) to work with God to support broken souls in a spirit of humility, not of haughtiness; for God asks His servants to work with Him (1 Cor 3:9) and to bear a spirit of humility, ascribing the fruit to God who works in them (1 Cor 3:7).

26.1.5.en: * Job answered and said: To whom do you give help? Is it to one who has no power? Or do you support the arm of one who is not strong? Here we need to know that we help even God, who is certainly not "without power," when we work in humility. Paul said: "We are labourers together with God" (1 Cor 9:3). If we contribute a voice of counsel to persons upon whom an inward grace is poured, we pass through with them by the Holy Spirit... We urge them toward perfection only when God is in the heart as a helper. Here too he says: "Neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase" (1 Cor 7:3). For he who plants or waters only helps, but the service is in vain unless God gives the increase in the heart.

26.1.6.en: But those who have haughty thoughts about the power of their own minds will not be helpers of God in humility, for they reckon themselves useful to God, and so make themselves strangers to profitable fruit.

26.1.7.en: * When pastors try to correct an erring flock, they must be adorned with humility, so that they do not stray in the use of their authority, and must feel that they are equal to the brethren whom they correct. And we pastors must train ourselves in silence and contemplation, and prefer the persons whose faults are being corrected to ourselves, because their sins have been corrected through us by hard training, whereas no one has rebuked us pastors for our own sins, even with a word. For this reason we pastors are judged before the Lord in proportion as we are released from punishment before men. And all the more is the flock freed from the divine judgment, because it is judged for its faults here in this world.

26.1.8.en: * Let the flock be assured that the pastors are inwardly humble before themselves. Thus the flock must understand what it ought to fear in authority and what it ought to imitate within the sphere of humility.

26.1.10.en: * It is plain that when one counsels another and at the same time suffers more than the one he rebukes, he does this not to cause grief to the other, but to offer him deep love. But he who rebukes another without this feeling in fact tramples with his feet upon his brother's feelings.

26.1.11.en: Father Ambrosiaster * Do not let the rank of the priesthood make you conceited, but rather let it make you humble, for dissolution and shame are born of haughtiness. The nearer you draw to the high ranks of the holy priestly order, the more it becomes you to be humble, remembering with fear the example of the sons of Aaron (Lev 10). The knowledge of the holy life is the knowledge of meekness and humility. Humility is the imitation of Christ. Arrogance, presumption and impudence are the imitation of Satan. Be an imitator of Christ, not of the antichrist; of God, not of the adversary of God; of the Master, not of the runaway slave; of the merciful, not of the merciless; of the Lover of mankind, not of its enemy; of your partner in the bridal chamber, not of the dweller in darkness. Do not be eager to exploit authority over the congregation, lest you place upon your neck the burdens of the sins of others.

26.2.0.en: St. Basil the Great How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom? and how hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is? [3]

26.2.1.en: Job rebukes Bildad because he offered theoretical philosophies, like one speaking to a child who has no wisdom, and displayed his understanding and knowledge with an abundance of words without action. He presented what is true, but he did not take the circumstances into account, so that the truth came out of place and out of season.

26.2.2.en: * "To whom hast thou given counsel? Perhaps to him that hath no wisdom?" [3] To give counsel to an ignorant man is a work of love; to give it to a wise man is boasting; but to give it to Wisdom Himself is a perversion of the mind.

26.2.3.en: * The shepherd of souls must discern wisely and carefully between the virtues and the vices, lest avarice take hold of his heart while he is excessive in appearing to be a good manager, or he boast of his generosity as though it were a virtue when he is in truth a squanderer and a waster; or he overlooks what he ought to criticize severely, and so brings eternal punishment upon his flock, or he punishes faults without mercy and so sins a greater sin, or he spoils what could have been done with dignity and uprightness by his hasty and reckless expectations. Likewise, postponing a good deed may turn it into an evil one.

26.3.0.en: To whom hast thou uttered words? and whose spirit came from thee? [4]

26.3.1.en: He says to him: [You have uttered words] out of place, for it was fitting for you to offer God's consolations to the tempted, not to terrify them with dreadful terrors. "And whose spirit came from thee?" That is, by what spirit are you animated to offer such talk to crush the wounded soul? It was fitting for you to seek wisdom and understanding from Him who gave you life and breath.

26.3.2.en: It was fitting for Bildad to say with the prophet Isaiah: "The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary" (Isa 50:4).

26.3.3.en: * "Whom do you wish to teach? Is it not He who made the way of the breath? By the breath we live, and by understanding we are wise. But we must first live, and afterward be dyed with wisdom, for in order that we may have the power to be wise, we must first possess Him who gave us life; He Himself, without doubt, grants us understanding also.

26.3.4.en: * Treatment at the wrong time makes wounds more painful. And if the medicines are unsuitable, they are certainly not fit for the purpose of healing.

26.3.6.en: * (The Apostle Paul) presented three marks of the preaching of the word: a burning, venturesome zeal; a soul ready to endure any dangers that may befall; and knowledge and wisdom joined together. For his love of venturing (in his preaching), and his blameless life, would have profited him nothing had he not received the power of the Spirit. Look at him as it appears in him first, or rather hear his words: "That the ministry be not blamed"(a).

26.4.s.en: 2. God's authority over the depths of the seas

26.4.0.en: The shades tremble beneath the waters and their inhabitants [5].

26.4.1.en: By the shades he means the huge, mighty creatures such as whales and sharks, which, though they live in the waters, fear God, as though God's care extends to the mighty, fierce creatures in the waters of the seas and oceans, over which He seems to have no authority. As it is said by the prophet Jeremiah: "Fear ye not me? saith the LORD: will ye not tremble at my presence, which have placed the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it: and though the waves thereof toss themselves, yet can they not prevail; though they roar, yet can they not pass over it?" (Jer 5:22).

26.4.2.en: Some think that the shades, or giants, here means those who in the days of Noah made light of him and thought that no evil would befall them, and who became as dwellers beneath the waters of the Flood that came upon them, and so were in trembling, but after it was too late!

26.4.3.en: * "Behold, the giants groan under the water" [5]. If by "giants" are meant those who hold power in this world, then the waters signify the multitudes, as John testifies by saying: [The waters which thou sawest are peoples] (Rev 15:17).

26.4.5.en: * Do you not see this sea, with its many waves and violent winds, and yet this vast, great sea, raging so, is held back by weak sand! Observe also the wisdom of God: He has allowed it no rest and no calm, lest you suppose that its good order is by a natural arrangement, and yet it keeps within its bounds. It lifts its voice high with its turmoil, its roaring, and its waves amazing in their height. But when they reach the shores, the sands hold them back and break them, and they return of themselves, in order that you may learn from all these things that it is not the work of mere nature that the sea stays within its bounds, but the work of Him who by His authority checks it! For this reason He made the barrier weak, and did not encircle the shores with timbers and stones and mountains, lest you ascribe the order of the elements to such things. Therefore God Himself trained the Jews in these very circumstances, saying: "Fear ye not me? saith the LORD... which have placed the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it" (Jer 5:22).

26.4.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * A grain of sand, the weakest of things, holds back the violence of the ocean.

26.5.0.en: Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering [6].

26.5.1.en: Job highlights the surpassing authority of God, that He is the Controller of all: He has authority over the huge, fierce creatures in the midst of the seas, and even over the devil and his angels who dwell in hell, for they are unable to do anything without His permission or leave.

26.5.2.en: Sheol is far from our sight, and the destruction that comes upon the demons and the wicked we have not yet seen, but everything is uncovered before the eyes of God, and He reveals it to whom He wills, such as His holy angels. It is said of him who worships the beast and his image and receives his mark on his forehead or on his hand: "The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb" (Rev 14:10).

26.5.3.en: Some think that Job is speaking of the wicked who have become sons of the devil and dwell with him in Sheol; these supposed that God did not see them, but they are exposed before the eyes of God. The Apostle says: "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13).

26.5.4.en: * [Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering] [6] Paul says something like it: [All things are naked and opened unto his eyes] (Heb 13:4). By hell and destruction he means Satan and all who are bound up with his judgment.

26.5.6.en: * Is it possible for God not to know such things, when there is no matter that escapes His care? "Hell is naked before his sight, and there is no covering for the wicked themselves," for they cannot hide.

26.5.7.en: St. Ambrose * (The word of God judges) the thoughts and intents of the heart, and there is no creature that is not manifest in his sight (Heb 4:12-13). With these words he terrifies them... He judges the inner heart, for in passing into it he punishes and searches it out. He says: And why do I speak of men? For even if you speak of the angels, and of the archangels, the Cherubim and Seraphim, or of any creature whatever, all is uncovered before that eye, all is plain and manifest, and nothing can escape from it.

26.5.8.en: * "All things are naked and opened" (Heb 4:13) to Him who judges us, and we are bound to give an account not only of words but also of thoughts, for this Judge quickly discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart.

26.5.9.en: * The righteous will shine forth as the sun, and even more than the sun, at that time; but the wicked will suffer all painful things to the utmost degree. There is no need there for records and proofs and witnesses, for the One who judges is everything: the witness, the proof and the judge, since He knows everything exactly: [All things are naked and opened unto his eyes].

26.5.10.en: St. John Chrysostom * "All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13). By this he means that He is other than all these (not a creature). Therefore it is He who judges, and each one of these is bound to give an account before Him.

26.6.0.en: 7 He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing. 8 He bindeth up the waters in his thick clouds; and the cloud is not rent under them. 9 He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it. 10 He hath compassed the waters with bounds, until the day and night come to an end. 11 The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his reproof. 12 He divideth the sea with his power, and by his understanding he smiteth through the proud.

26.6.1.en: He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing [7].

26.6.2.en: Holy Scripture likens God the Creator to one who spreads out the heavens and the earth, and who remains in His care for His creation, spreading out both until the times come to an end and He folds them up. The psalmist says: "Who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain"(b). And as it is written in the Book of Revelation: "The heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together" (Rev 6:14). As for his choosing "the north," it is because Job lives in the northern hemisphere, and so sees God spreading out the earth as over an empty place, that is, as though it were empty or as nothing when compared with the other world. The psalmist says: "The north and the south thou hast created them" (Ps 89:12).

26.6.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that the north signifies Satan, whose kingdom is empty of God's grace. Even the kingdom of the devil is not hidden from God.

26.6.4.en: * The Lord gave the earth stability, and it will remain so as long as God wills it.

26.6.5.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * Who ought not to be amazed and perplexed at these things, declaring with certainty that they are not the work of nature, but of the divine providence that surpasses nature? For one says: [Who hangeth the earth upon nothing] (Job 7:26). And another: [In his hand are the deep places of the earth] (Ps 4:95).

26.6.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * "He stretcheth out the north over the empty place" [7]. "The north" is used in Holy Scripture to signify Satan... for he (Satan) reigns over those whose hearts are not filled with the grace of the love of God. But Almighty God is able to fill even the vessels of Satan, empty of every virtue, with the gift of His grace, and to place the fear of God in those persons whom He sees established in no conduct of righteousness. Therefore he rightly added: "And hangeth the earth upon nothing." For what does he mean by the earth, if not the Holy Church? It receives the words of preaching and brings forth the fruit of good works. Moses said of it: [Hear, O earth, the words of my mouth... let my speech distil as the rain] (Deut 32:1-2). And what is "nothing," if not the many peoples of the Gentiles, of whom the prophet says: [All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing] (cf. Isa 17:40).

26.6.8.en: "He hangeth the earth upon nothing." He created the earth and set it up without pillars. There is nothing that a man can hang upon nothing, but God established the whole earth upon nothing. And as the Apostle says: "Upholding all things by the word of his power" (Heb 1:3). He who set up the globe of the earth and established it, that man might walk on it and live, can He not by the word of His power order the whole life of man?

26.6.9.en: * You set up the heaven for me as a roof, and You established the earth for me to walk upon.

26.6.10.en: For my sake You bridled the sea, for my sake You showed forth the nature of the animals, You put everything under my feet. You did not leave me lacking in any of the works of Your honor.

26.7.0.en: The Liturgy of St. Gregory the Theologian He bindeth up the waters in his thick clouds; and the cloud is not rent under them [8].

26.7.1.en: God keeps the waters of which it was said that they are "above the firmament" (Gen 1:7), so that they are not poured out in a single flood to drown the world, as happened in the days of Noah. They are kept (bound up) by divine wisdom. He lets them fall as rains by a well-ordered divine arrangement and in a set measure, so that, with all the weight of these waters that have become clouds, the clouds beneath them are not rent so that they fall all at once, for the benefit of those who dwell on the earth, men and animals and crops.

26.7.2.en: St. John Chrysostom stands amazed before God's surpassing providence, in that He allows the water (in the clouds) to be carried up above the air, and God seals it with the air, so that it runs to many places to water the earth.

26.7.3.en: * Who is it that "bindeth up the waters in the clouds"? It is a wonder that He places something that by its nature overflows so that it stays in the cloud, holding it fast by His word. But He pours out a part of it upon the face of the earth, letting it fall in drops at the proper time. He does not let loose the whole store of waters, but is content with the cleansing that was accomplished in the days of Noah. God remains true to His covenant.

26.7.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a symbolic interpretation, seeing in the waters a symbol of knowledge, and in the thick cloud the company of the preachers, for it is God who grants the preachers heavenly knowledge.

26.7.5.en: If Bildad and his two companions claim wisdom and knowledge, it is fitting for them to be like the light cloud that flies in the sky and rises above dust and earthly things, so that they may enjoy heavenly wisdom and divine knowledge.

26.7.6.en: God in His surpassing providence grants us by His grace to become a cloud, or a divine chariot, as the prophet Isaiah said: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift (bright) cloud, and shall come into Egypt" (Isa 19:1). By dwelling in us He fills us with His knowledge, His wisdom and His love, and flies with us as though to Egypt, that is, to the heart of every man, that we may present to them the One who dwells in us, God, the true Love!

26.7.7.en: * "He bindeth up the waters in his thick cloud, so that they burst not downward" [8]. What does he signify by the waters in this place but knowledge, and by the cloud but the preachers? For water in Holy Scripture is sometimes used to signify knowledge, as Solomon teaches us, bearing witness to it. He says: [The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook] (Prov 4:18). And the prophet David bears witness that waters signify knowledge, saying that the dark waters are in the clouds of the sky, and the hidden mysteries, since they carried within them boundless mysteries, whose meanings are obscure in the eyes of those who behold them.

26.7.8.en: And what does the name "cloud" signify in this passage but the holy preachers, that is, the Apostles, who were sent out in every direction to the ends of the world, who know how to rain with words and to flash lightning with miracles? Isaiah looked upon them long ago and said: [Who are these that fly as a cloud?] (Isa 8:60).

26.7.10.en: * "His lightnings enlightened the world" (Ps 97:4). This is great joy... His lightnings shine over all the world: His enemies sit upon fire and are burned... How do the lightnings shine? By the world's believing. Where do the lightnings come from? From the cloud. And what is the cloud of God? The preachers of the truth... Our Lord Jesus Christ sent His Apostles out as preachers like clouds. They were seen as men and were despised, and yet they appeared as clouds.

26.7.11.en: St. Augustine * Virtue is a thing bright and joyful, and those who live in its way fly like a cloud, as Isaiah says: [And as the doves to their windows] (Isa 60:8). But sin is like something heavy and sitting still, as another prophet says: "a talent of lead" (Zech 5:8).

26.7.12.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa St. Basil the Great sees that all men are like clouds, ever in motion, moving as the winds direct them. He whom the wind of the Lord moves goes forth toward heaven, but he who leaves himself to the winds of the world and the passions moves toward hell for his destruction.

26.7.13.en: * Men are like clouds, moving here and there in the sky according to the changes of the winds.

26.8.0.en: St. Basil the Great He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it [9].

26.8.1.en: It is out of God's love for us and His wonderful care that He veils the face of His throne, so that we do not see Him as He is, because, as He said: "There shall no man see me, and live" (Ex 33:20). He spreads cloud and mist over it, so that He appears as in obscurity, since our eyes are unable to behold Him, and we live by faith and not by sight, until we meet Him face to face on the great day of the Lord, as much as we are able to bear.

26.8.2.en: * The face of his throne is veiled, which means that we do not perceive the glory of His kingdom in this life. For while His greatness is within, He spreads His cloud, because the glory of the heavenly kingdom is not seen as it is. For [the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that museth upon many things] (Wis 15:9). So the mist is spread over us, and we do not see His glory, being darkened by the cloud of our ignorance. Rightly does the psalmist say: [Darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind. He made darkness his secret place] (cf. Ps 9:18-11)...

26.8.3.en: But if we reckon His throne to be the angelic powers, since He sits upon these very powers as upon a royal throne, He turns the face of His throne away from us, for as long as we have the mortal body we do not perceive the wonder of the ministry of the angels, nor how it is carried out.

26.8.4.en: "And spreadeth his cloud upon it," since He lifts up our heart to search; and the heart passes through in a hidden way, so that for all its endless searching it is turned back. So it is written: [The deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high] (Hab 10:3).

26.8.6.en: * [He bowed the heavens also, and came down: and darkness was under his feet] (Ps 18:9). This is the humility of the Righteous One, who bowed down because of the weakness of men.

26.8.7.en: "And darkness was under his feet." Those whose wickedness has blinded their eyes; these wicked, who care only for earthly things, cannot know Him, for the earth falls under His feet, bound to the footstool.

26.8.8.en: St. Augustine * Every mind, according to the measure of its stature, is enlightened with a limited quantity of light.

26.8.9.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * The face of God is the impress of His substance (Heb 3:1). He who desires the face of God with all his heart, so that he is able to contemplate it with a pure heart and to fix his gaze upon it, shall be shown mercy, according to the Lord's saying. Such a man is able to utter the words that are before us.

26.8.10.en: How great is he who sees the face of God! Let the Lord Jesus teach you his greatness, as He says: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God" (Mt 8:5).

26.9.0.en: St. Didymus the Blind He hath compassed the waters with bounds, until the day and night come to an end [10].

26.9.1.en: Job looks upon the vast seas and sees the rivers pouring into them, and yet their waters do not increase so as to overflow the land; rather, the sands, small grains as they are, stand as a barrier that holds them back. Thus God granted the seas to respect the earth, so that they do not overflow the earth with their waters.

26.9.2.en: If the waters of the seas know their limits and do not pass them, it is fitting for the peoples and nations (the many waters) to respect others, so that no nation oppresses another, and no man another.

26.9.3.en: * As for the sea, if I am not astonished at its greatness, I must be astonished at its nobility: What bounds it? How does it rise and then grow calm at the end, like one who respects his neighbor "the earth"? How does it receive into itself all the rivers, and remain as it is, in spite of the overflowing of its huge being, if one may say so...? How is its limit set by an element such as sand alone...? "He hath set a bound upon the face of the waters by his commandment" (Job 10:26) LXX.

26.9.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * "He setteth bounds to the waters until the light and the darkness come to an end" [10]. As we said before, the peoples are signified in Holy Scripture by the waters. The Lord sets bounds to the waters when He deals with human knowledge, so that it does not attain perfectly to the knowledge of the inner splendor until the succession of changing seasons has passed away.

26.9.5.en: If we understand by the light the righteous, and by the darkness sinners, Paul says: [Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light] (Eph 8:5), then nothing prevents us from understanding that the perfect knowledge of eternity is given to no one until the course of the righteous and the course of the wicked comes to an end.

26.10.0.en: The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his reproof [11].

26.10.1.en: * What are the pillars of heaven but the holy angels, the chief preachers of the Church, upon whom the whole heavenly world of the spiritual edifice, rising without ceasing, is established, as Holy Scripture says in another place: "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God" (Rev 3:12). For he who is firmly established, with a sound aim in his mind, in the work of God stands as a pillar in the building of the spiritual edifice. Being set in this temple, which is the Church, he becomes both a use and an adornment. But Job calls those "pillars of heaven" whom the Apostle calls pillars of the Church, saying: [Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me the right hand of fellowship] (Gal 9:2).

26.10.2.en: It is not unfitting to interpret the "pillars of heaven" as the churches themselves. For though they are many in number, they constitute one catholic (universal) Church spread over all the face of the earth. So also the Apostle John writes to the seven churches, meaning the one catholic Church supplied with the Spirit, whose grace is sevenfold...

26.10.3.en: Now the very powers of the heavenly world, who see Him without ceasing and for whom He is the object of contemplation, have become filled with dread. But it is not the dread of woe, since it is not the dread of fear, but the dread of wonder. For having brought such great dread by His wondrous work, He now recounts to us the dispensation of our salvation.

26.11.0.en: He divideth the sea with his power, and by his understanding he smiteth through Rahab [12].

26.11.1.en: Some scholars, who reckon that Job lived in the days of the prophet Moses or after him, think that he is speaking here of God's work with His people, in that by His power He divided the Red Sea, and by His understanding He crushed Egypt, since the word "Rahab" is often used to express Egypt (Ps 87:4; Isa 51:9).

26.11.2.en: * "By his power the seas were gathered together suddenly, and his wisdom shook the proud" [12]. What does the sea signify but the present world, in which the hearts of men seek earthly things and are swollen with the surges of conflicting thoughts? For being stirred up by the arrogance of pride, and opposing one another in the passage of the waves, they shatter themselves together against the currents. But "by his power the seas were gathered together," for when the Lord became incarnate, the opposing hearts of worldly men believed and came into agreement...

26.11.3.en: Who is he who is here called the proud, if not he who said: [I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High] (Isa 14:14)? The voice of God said of him: [Who made himself to fear no one, and set himself up as king over all the children of pride](c). The prophet David agrees with this passage, saying: ["Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces, as one that is slain"] (cf. Ps 10:89).

26.12.s.en: 5. God, the mystery of the heavens' beauty

26.12.0.en: By his spirit the heavens are clear, and his hands have formed the fleeing serpent [13].

26.12.1.en: In the translation of the Jesuits it reads, "By his spirit he adorned the heavens." By His Holy Spirit He established the heavens and adorned them with the stars by night and with the sun by day.

26.12.2.en: Some Fathers of the Church hold that man, unlike the animals, looks upward and not downward, and that the Spirit of God adorned the heavens in order to draw man's gaze to the heights, so that he would not be occupied with earthly things. He set up for him the visible heavens, wonderfully made, so that by faith he might look to the invisible heavens, awaiting his eternal dwelling.

26.12.3.en: In some translations the phrase reads "the crooked serpent." If God is the Creator of the heavens and the giver to them of this wonderful adornment, He is also the Creator of the animals, even the serpent that became crooked. Some think that he means here the whale or the crocodile, and others that he means "leviathan the piercing serpent" (Isa 27:1). He is the Creator and good in His gifts, but He grants free will to the rational creation, so the devil, by his evil will and disobedience, became the old crooked serpent.

26.12.4.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that God the Father drew out by His hand (the incarnate Wisdom of God) the crooked serpent from its authority, for on the Cross He stripped it of its authority and made a show of it (Col 2:15). So by the Holy Spirit our souls fly as though to the heavens prepared for us in all their splendor, and by the Cross of the Lord of glory we tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy. He grants us the heavenly life, and He grants us victory over the devil and all his powers.

26.12.5.en: * "His hand brought forth the crooked serpent" [13]. Who is described as the serpent (and the stubborn dragon) but our ancient enemy, the cunning and crooked one, who spoke with the mouth of a serpent to deceive man? It is said of him by the prophet: [Leviathan the crooked serpent] (Isa 1:27). He was permitted to speak with the mouth of a serpent, so that man might learn by this who it is that dwells in it...

26.12.6.en: By the hand of the Lord the crooked serpent was drawn out of its hole, so that by the healing divine grace our ancient enemy who reigned over us is driven out from us. The incarnate Truth says: [Now shall the prince of this world be cast out] (Jn 31:12). Now he no longer possesses the saints, holding them fast, but he persecutes them with trials. For he has no possession within them, but wages war against them from outside... He has lost his authority within, and so he raises up wars from without.

26.13.s.en: 6. How rich is the greatness of God

26.13.0.en: Lo, these are parts of his ways: and how low is the word that we hear of him!

26.13.1.en: But the thunder of his power who can understand? [14]

26.13.2.en: Here Job ends his speech, confessing God's love for man, for He reveals "the outskirts of his ways," or a portion of His wisdom, His power and His plan, as much as man can bear or grasp. But however much knowledge of God's mysteries we attain, it is counted as the least of the least of what He wishes to reveal to us. We hear a faint whisper of His words. "How low is the word that we hear of him!" We still [know in part, and prophesy in part] (1 Cor 13:9). We sing with the Apostle Paul, saying: "How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!" (Rom 11:33). It is impossible for us, while still in this world, to reach the depths of the knowledge and wisdom of God, for we see Him as in a mirror, in a riddle, until we meet Him face to face in the age to come (1 Cor 13:12). So the little that we receive is counted as a great and exceedingly fearful thunder, "but the thunder of his power who can understand?"

26.13.3.en: St. Ambrose holds that when God speaks, He thunders, because man, in his inability to grasp the mysteries of God, stands amazed before the divine speech, like one before a thunder whose secret cannot be grasped.

26.13.4.en: * It is most fitting that (Christ) should establish thunders by His coming, I mean the power and voice of the holy heavenly Scriptures, as a kind of thunder. That is, our minds are struck with amazement, and learn that we fear and dread the heavenly utterances greatly.

26.13.5.en: Finally, in the Gospel the brethren of the Lord were called "sons of thunder," and when the voice of the Father spoke, saying to the Son: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again" (Jn 12:28), the Jews said: "It thundered." Though they were unable to receive the grace of the truth, they confessed involuntarily, and without knowing it spoke of the mystery of the great testimony of the Father about the Son. In the Book of Job also the Scripture says: "Who knoweth when he will make the power of his thunder" (Job 26:14) LXX.

26.13.6.en: St. Ambrose * Men see Him in the measure that they die to this world, and in the measure that they live to it they do not see Him. And although this light begins to appear clearly, not only more possible to see but also more delightful, yet it is seen as in a dark mirror (a riddle). So we say that we see Him because we walk by faith, not by sight, while we wander in this world as strangers, even if our conversation is in heaven (1 Cor 12:13; 2 Cor 7:5). At this stage a man washes the eyes of his affections to see that he has not set his neighbor before him... for in truth he has not yet loved him as himself.

26.13.7.en: * This vision is kept as a reward for our faith, of which the Apostle John says: "When he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 2:3). We understand the "face" of God as His revelation, not a part of the body similar to that in our bodies which we call by this name.

26.13.8.en: St. Augustine * "Lo, these things are spoken of his ways in part, and since we hardly hear a little drop of his words, who can look upon the thunder of his greatness?" [14] What does he mean here by defining His ways but the Lord's ways of working? So also the Lord says by the prophet: [For my ways are not your ways] (Isa 8:55). Therefore, in telling of the coming of the Lord, he describes the ways of God in part. The means of working by which He created us is different from that by which He saved us. Thus he has told us of those things that belong to the Lord's way of working, (disclosing) them by comparing them with the last judgment. He says: "Lo, these things are spoken of his ways in part." These also he called "a little drop of his words," for by contemplating Him while we are in this life we come to know His loftiness and awesomeness...

26.13.9.en: "Who can look upon the thunder of his greatness?" [14] It is as though he expresses himself in plain words: If we can hardly bear the wonders of His humility, with what boldness shall we face the coming (or appearing) of His exalted and awesome majesty? The psalmist also describes the thunder of His coming, saying: [Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him] (Ps 3:50).

26.13.11.en: * We know ourselves through reflection, as in a mirror. As far as we are able, we contemplate the Creator Cause through the divine element in us.

26.13.13.en: Your works bear witness to Your greatness and Your love!

26.13.14.en: * Your works, O Almighty, Lover of mankind, bear witness to You.

26.13.15.en: You did not establish this wonderful world to display Your power, but to embrace every man with Your works of love.

26.13.16.en: Grant me, as Your child, not to be occupied with theology in dryness.

26.13.17.en: But I ask for fellowship with You, that my heart may be enlarged with love for all men!

26.13.18.en: Grant me not to criticize anyone, but let my depths groan over my own weakness, and have compassion on the weaknesses of my brethren.

26.13.19.en: Let me cleave to You, and so love every man!

26.13.20.en: * Let me work through You and with Your grace, so that I bear the spirit of humility.

26.13.21.en: I work, but it is You who work in me, so that I know neither sloth nor indifference, nor do I know haughtiness and pride and self-righteousness.

26.13.22.en: Let me cry out with Your wonderful Apostle Paul:

26.13.24.en: * Grant me the wisdom that comes down from above, that I may not display dry philosophical talk, nor offer counsel out of season, nor make light of the one with whom I speak!

26.13.25.en: Grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may walk as is fitting.

26.13.26.en: Let me bring the spirit of hope to every tempted soul.

26.13.27.en: Let me offer Your consolations to every wounded heart.

26.13.28.en: Let me know how to be firm with sincere love, and loving without laxity.

26.13.29.en: Grant me what You granted to Your Apostle Paul:

26.13.30.en: A burning zeal, and a soul that endures suffering, with wisdom and knowledge!

26.13.31.en: * For my sake You created these oceans, and with all their might and the might of the creatures in them, grains of sand hold them back from invading the land where I dwell.

26.13.32.en: You set the seas their bounds with small, weak sand!

26.13.33.en: * You are the Controller of all!

26.13.34.en: You have authority over the fierce creatures in the midst of the seas, You have authority over the devil and Sheol.

26.13.35.en: Everything is naked before You, so why should I fear, when You are my loving Shepherd?

26.13.36.en: What I fear is my negligence and my heedlessness of Your care!

26.13.37.en: * For my sake You created the globe of the earth and established it, this that seems to be hung upon nothing, yet is kept by Your divine care.

26.13.38.en: In wisdom You keep the waters as a moving cloud, that they may become rain for our good.

26.13.39.en: * Grant me to become like a light cloud, moved by love, that my depths may rain with the showers of Your wisdom, and water many.

26.13.40.en: * Your love permitted the mist around You.

26.13.41.en: Lest we see You while we are in the earthly body, and die.

26.13.42.en: But You promised us that we shall see You face to face.

26.13.43.en: When will this wonderful meeting come to pass?

26.13.44.en: * The seas into which the rivers pour their waters know their limits, and so respect their neighbor, the dry land.

26.13.45.en: Grant the peoples and nations that all may respect their neighbors and know their limits!

26.13.46.en: * Raise up from among Your servants pillars of spiritual, heavenly joy.

26.13.47.en: That they may bear witness to Your wonderful and awesome works.

26.13.48.en: That they may preach Your salvation.

26.13.49.en: You brought Your people across the Red Sea, and crushed Pharaoh and his army!

26.13.50.en: Bring us across to Your Kingdom, and shatter the heads of the dragon in the waters of Baptism!

26.13.51.en: * You stretched out Your hand on the Cross, and shattered the deadly serpent, our ancient enemy!

26.13.52.en: You drove it out of our hearts so that You may return to Your dwelling, O Holy One.

26.13.53.en: * Shine in me with Your light, that I may meditate on the works of Your surpassing love.

26.13.54.en: Thunder within me, that I may enjoy Your mysteries!
